text: Every chapter in this course has been building toward this. Chapters one through nine gave you a methodology, execution-plan literacy, index design, query-rewrite technique, wait-stat analysis, tempdb and memory tuning, Query Store, and configuration tuning. This chapter is a single continuous scenario spread across six lessons, where you apply all of it to one genuinely slow production database -- start to finish, the way it actually happens on the job.

Meridian Outfitters is a mid-size outdoor gear retailer. Its order system lives in a database called MeridianRetail, and support reps use an internal CRM called MeridianConnect to look up a customer's order history. Three years ago dbo dot Orders held about two million rows; today it holds roughly fourteen million, partly organic growth, but mostly a B2B wholesale program launched eighteen months ago. The screen reps use is powered by one stored procedure -- a single filtered, sorted SELECT against dbo dot Orders, filtering on CustomerID and the trailing twelve months, ordered by OrderDate descending. Nothing exotic.

Support tickets don't arrive as the database is slow. They arrive as this: starting about six weeks ago, reps began reporting the Order History panel sometimes spins for twenty to thirty seconds before timing out -- the app gives up at thirty. It's worst between ten AM and two PM Eastern, Meridian's peak call-center hours, and it's not every customer -- most lookups are still instant. Wholesale accounts like TrailWorks Co-op, CustomerID forty-eight thousand two-thirteen, place thousands of orders a year instead of a consumer's handful. Intermittent, load-correlated, and concentrated on specific accounts -- that's a real clue, not noise.

It would be easy to guess right now: probably a missing index, probably tempdb contention at this database size. Chapter one's loop exists precisely to stop you from acting on a guess. Before this chapter is done, you'll gather a real baseline, read the actual execution plan, check real wait statistics, and only then make one deliberate, measured change.

The next lesson starts exactly there -- measuring, not fixing. Query Store's own history, the actual execution plan for TrailWorks Co-op's lookup, and the real wait stats behind it are all about to turn a vague symptom into a named bottleneck.
